intervals.label: construction and installation
intervals.locator: INSPIRE experiment record 1110643, fields date_approved and date_completed
intervals.note: Start = date_approved (1998-09-17). End = INSPIRE's date_completed field, which reads '2008-09'. That field is not a routine construction-milestone field: on ATLAS's INSPIRE record (1108541) and on LHCf's (1126263) the same field reads '9999', which both records treat as INSPIRE's placeholder for 'ongoing, not completed' rather than a real date. LHCb is likewise an active, non-terminal experiment, so a literal 'completed' date is implausible; the value is most likely either an INSPIRE data-entry anomaly or a differently scoped milestone (for example detector installation or construction complete, consistent with first collisions 14 months later). No source independent of this one INSPIRE field corroborates a September 2008 construction-complete date for LHCb, so confidence is 'uncertain' and the interval is given the non-terminal status 'construction', not 'completed'; it must not be read as asserting that LHCb completed in 2008. The LHCb JINST detector paper or an LHCb-specific installation announcement would settle it.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 2 / LHCb Upgrade I installation
intervals.note: The LHC-wide Long Shutdown 2 ended and Run 3 pp collisions began on 5 July 2022 (see accelerator:lhc), but LHCb's own outreach page dates the completion of Upgrade I installation to April 2023, nine months later. This interval follows the LHCb-specific completion date, since Upgrade I (new VELO, new tracker, removal of the hardware trigger) is an LHCb-specific programme. The gap likely reflects LHCb running in a partial or commissioning capacity for the first months of Run 3 while installation finished; no source consulted states this explicitly.
intervals.quote: The installation of the new Upgrade I detector was completed in April 2023.

intervals.note: Start = LHCb Upgrade I installation completion (see previous interval); end = the LHC-wide switch-off for Long Shutdown 3 (accelerator:lhc).

end.note: CERN schedule: the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030; the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from mid-2028.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3 / ECAL and RICH enhancements
intervals.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, item of 5 August 2026 "The LHC is being warmed up from near absolute zero to room temperature"
intervals.note: LHCb's own detector is being enhanced in this shutdown: the inner part of the electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is replaced and the RICH electronics are upgraded. LHCb's outreach site (8 May 2024) says 'The LHCb experiment will upgrade the inner part of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter and the electronics of the Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors in the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3)'. The LHCb ECAL group's JINST paper (published 11 March 2026) says 'An enhancement of the LHCb electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) is foreseen during Long Shutdown 3 (LS3) of the LHC' and 'In total, 176 new SpaCal modules with radiation-tolerant scintillating plastic fibers will be installed during LS3'. These are plans for the shutdown; no source consulted reports the installation as under way or finished. The main Upgrade II is a later step: 'Upgrade II will be installed during Long Shutdown 4 (LS4)' (LHCb outreach site, 2024). The 2024 page gives LS3 as 'currently scheduled for the years 2026–28'; this interval follows CERN's later schedule, in which the LHC resumes operation in mid-2030. Start and end are the LHC-wide Long Shutdown 3 dates. CERN's 5 August 2026 item says 'The cryogenics team has been running the warm-up sequence since LS3 began on 29 June 2026' and that the stored helium is kept 'ready to be used again once the accelerator resumes operation in mid-2030'; CERN's 29 June 2026 article says 'The HiLumi LHC, scheduled to begin operation in 2030'. The end is a schedule value, not a reported event.
intervals.quote: The LHCb experiment will upgrade the inner part of the Electromagnetic Calorimeter and the electronics of the Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors in the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3).

physics_goals.quote: The Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment specializes in investigating the slight differences between matter and antimatter by studying a type of particle called the "beauty quark", or "b quark".
physics_goals.value: Study CP violation and rare decays of b (beauty) and c (charm) hadrons to probe the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe

summary.plain: LHCb is one of the four big experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Instead of surrounding the collision point on all sides, its detector is shaped like a single forward cone, built to catch particles containing beauty and charm quarks and study why the universe has so much more matter than antimatter.
summary.technical: Single-arm forward-spectrometer experiment at LHC Point 8 (Ferney-Voltaire, France), covering low pseudorapidity in the forward direction to exploit the strongly forward-peaked production of b-hadrons and c-hadrons at hadron colliders. Proposed by Letter of Intent in August 1995, approved September 1998, installed by September 2008, first collisions November 2009. Physics programme centres on CP violation and rare decays of heavy-flavour hadrons; Upgrade I (new VELO, silicon tracker, removal of the hardware trigger) was installed by April 2023.

unique_capabilities.quote: Instead of surrounding the entire collision point with an enclosed detector as do ATLAS and CMS, the LHCb experiment uses a series of subdetectors to detect mainly forward particles - those thrown forwards by the collision in one direction.
unique_capabilities.value: A single forward-arm spectrometer (not a 4π enclosure) optimised for the forward-peaked production of b and c hadrons at a hadron collider
